It built analytics software that helps online merchants and financial institutions score transaction risk by email address. It was a software company that ran on cloud and outsourced infrastructure rather than one that operated its own colocation or hosting facility, and a check of the address on file today finds a different, unrelated tenant in place. Nothing publicly available ties this specific address to server or data center infrastructure, and this entry does not present a software company's former office as a data center facility.

reading.body:
A mistagged OpenStreetMap point for a former software office should not be counted in Arizona's AI infrastructure.

Emailage was a fraud-prevention and email-risk-scoring software company, acquired by LexisNexis Risk Solutions. It consumed cloud infrastructure rather than operating any. The coordinates on file now resolve to a different tenant, Safe T Professionals LLC, at 25 South Arizona Place in Chandler. Nothing ties this address to servers or hosting.

The error matters because facility counts feed the map of where compute physically sits. Arizona has 56 mapped facilities, and only 4 carry published capacity figures, totaling 512 MW. A phantom entry inflates the first number while leaving the second untouched, which is the worse outcome: it suggests more sites than the state can account for with real power data.

What this does not tell the reader is anything about Emailage's actual infrastructure, because none is documented here. It also says nothing about the other 55 Arizona facilities, which are several miles away and unconnected to this address. The entry is one bad point, not evidence of a broader pattern.
